rationale_summary: New York's RAISE Act is overwhelmingly framed around existential and catastrophic risk, orienting every substantive protocol, evaluation, deployment prohibition, third-party audit, incident report, and whistleblower protection toward preventing 'critical harm'—defined as 100 or more deaths or serious injuries or at least $1 billion in damages enabled through chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons or frontier models acting autonomously with limited human intervention to commit serious crimes, alongside loss-of-control evasion, self-creation of new frontier models, and model-weight escape. Consumer and public safety provides a secondary rationale through explicit public-safety redaction criteria, mass-casualty and property-damage prevention, and public transparency of safety protocols and audit reports. A minor national security dimension enters via protection of frontier model weights against sophisticated actors and routing oversight and 72-hour incident disclosures through the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services.
